summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang, Tianzuo Li, Jiyeon Lee, Dahye Lim, Lianjie Xu, Yajie Liu, Jongcheol Seo, Wen-Bin Zhang
summary.executive_summary: This study reports the design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), a mechanically interlocked polypeptide structure that is extremely rare in nature. The authors achieved this by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, using the original fold as the entangling template. The synthesis was accomplished in cells using a series of programmed streamlined post-translational processing events involving mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs, without additional in vitro reactions. The resulting cat-DHFR was thoroughly characterized using LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to the linear control (l-DHFR), cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability, although with reduced activity (~5 U/mg vs ~14 U/mg) and lower substrate affinity. However, cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability against thermal and chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction imposed by the mechanical interlocking. The study demonstrates that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents a new horizon in protein science, offering a unique scaffold for further engineering and evolution, and highlighting topology as a distinct dimension for protein design.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), a mechanically interlocked polypeptide structure that is extremely rare in nature. The authors achieved this by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, using the original fold as the entangling template. The synthesis was accomplished in cells using a series of programmed streamlined post-translational processing events involving mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs, without additional in vitro reactions. The resulting cat-DHFR was thoroughly characterized using LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to the linear control (l-DHFR), cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability, although with reduced activity (~5 U/mg vs ~14 U/mg) and lower substrate affinity. However, cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability against thermal and chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction imposed by the mechanical interlocking. The study demonstrates that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents a new horizon in protein science, offering a unique scaffold for further engineering and evolution, and highlighting topology as a distinct dimension for protein design.

Research Context
Natural protein domains are based on linear polypeptide chains with limited topological diversity. The discovery of natural topological proteins suggests unconventional topology could enhance stability. Topology has been recognized as a unique dimension for protein engineering. Previous artificial topological proteins often contain multiple domains, complicating structure-property studies. Ideally, a single-domain topological protein would exhibit the most profound impact of chemical topology. It remains challenging to prepare single-domain topological proteins, even for the simplest catenane. The need for exogenous entangling motifs may be eliminated by exploiting spatially entangled relationships. The goal is to design single-domain protein catenanes with identical composition to linear wild-type.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a single-domain protein catenane can be designed and synthesized. The hypothesis is that rewiring connectivity between secondary motifs can introduce artificial entanglement. It is hypothesized that using the original fold as a template allows synthesis without exogenous motifs. The predicted outcome is a catenane with preserved function and elevated stability. The study aims to demonstrate the feasibility of converting DHFR into its catenane counterpart. It is expected that the catenane will retain catalytic capability despite topological changes. The design should ensure entangled conformation and high reconstitution efficiency. The active site and adjacent regions should be left intact to preserve activity.

Methodological Details
The study utilized dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) from Escherichia coli as the model enzyme. The design involved rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs. The Gaussian linking number (GLN) matrix was used to identify splitting positions. Cleavage at residues 88 and 89 generated two highly intertwined segments. The design consisted of residues 1-88 as one ring and 89-159 as the other. Synthesis used two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs. Ring I was circularly permutated to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24. The rewired loops were designed to be 16 residues long. A TEV protease recognition sequence was included for topology proof. A linear control (l-DHFR) with identical amino acid composition was designed. Genes were sub-cloned into pMCSG19 and pET21a vectors. Proteins were expressed in E. coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. Expression was carried out at 16 °C for 20 hours. Purification was performed using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography and size exclusion chromatography. Characterization included LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry.

Procedures And Architectures
The retrosynthetic analysis guided the choice of ring closure sites. Cyclization efficiency depends on the distance between new termini. The two bulky split-intein pairs were placed on opposite sides to avoid interference. The gene cassette contained two DHFR segments and two split-intein pairs. Protein expression was optimized for proper folding and complete reaction. SDS-PAGE showed a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR. The faster mobility of cat-DHFR in SDS-PAGE indicates a more compact structure. SEC showed cat-DHFR elutes as a broader peak at a larger retention volume. LC-MS confirmed the accurate molecular weights of cat-DHFR and l-DHFR. Far-UV CD spectra showed reduced intensities of positive and negative peaks. Near-UV CD spectrum exhibited positive ellipticity at ~290 nm. Proteolytic digestion with TEV protease converted cat-DHFR to linear and cyclic fragments. Ion mobility spectrometry and collision-induced dissociation were used for topology proof. Kinetic parameters Km and kcat were determined by Michaelis curve fitting. Binding affinity was determined using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC).

Key Results
cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability with an activity of ~5 U/mg. The linear control l-DHFR has an activity of ~14 U/mg. cat-DHFR has a Km approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR. The kcat of cat-DHFR is about 38% that of l-DHFR. The catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) of cat-DHFR is reduced by an order of magnitude. The dissociation constant for DHF is ~173-fold larger for cat-DHFR. The dissociation constant for NADPH is ~14-fold larger for cat-DHFR. The dissociation constant for THF is ~3.6-fold larger for cat-DHFR. cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability against thermal denaturation. cat-DHFR preserved 87% activity in 5% DMSO, compared to 74% for l-DHFR. The GLN of cat-DHFR is +1.120. The GLN of the split DHFR segments is +0.726. The yield with the shortest linker is about one-fifth that of the longest. The yield with the longest linker is ~12 mg/L of culture.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Mechanical interlocking enhances the thermal resilience of the enzyme. The reduced activity is attributed to compromised affinity towards substrate and cofactor. Circular permutation causes minor local disturbance but overall structure is intact. The catenane topology reinforces the folded structure. This approach offers a new horizon in protein science. Linear proteins can be converted into concatenated counterparts with preserved function. Topology provides a unique dimension for protein engineering. The design allows for further engineering and evolution of the scaffold.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors failed to obtain a crystal structure of cat-DHFR. The lack of crystal structure limits unambiguous proof of topology. The approach requires extensive optimization for high-yield expression. Steric hindrance of split-intein pairs affects reconstitution efficiency. Shorter linkers lead to decreased yield and increased by-products. The reduced activity may be further restored by directed evolution. The dynamic structure of cat-DHFR suggests coupled movement of rings.

Claims
A single-domain protein catenane of DHFR can be synthesized in cells without in vitro reactions. Synthesis was accomplished by programmed post-translational processing. No additional in vitro reactions were required. The method uses orthogonal split-intein pairs. The process requires extensive optimization. Side products can form if linkers are too short. This enables the study of topological effects on single domains. It provides a new scaffold for protein engineering.
cat-DHFR retains catalytic function but with reduced activity and affinity. cat-DHFR has ~5 U/mg activity. Km is 5-fold higher than linear control. kcat is 38% of linear control. Previous rethreaded DHFR showed no activity. Split DHFR complex retained only 15% activity. Function is preserved despite topological change. Activity can potentially be restored by evolution.
cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability against thermal and chemical denaturation. Enhanced stability against thermal denaturation. 87% activity preserved in 5% DMSO. Mechanical interlocking enhances resilience. Secondary structure intensities are reduced. Topology can be used to stabilize proteins. This is a new dimension for protein design.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The method is robust before the linker becomes too short. Shorter linkers lead to decreased yield and more by-products. Circular permutation was necessary to place cyclization motifs on opposite sides. Different sites for ring closure were tested. The site between residues 23 and 24 was most efficient.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the molecular design and retrosynthetic analysis. Figure 2 shows SDS-PAGE, SEC, LC-MS, and CD spectra. Figure 4c shows kinetic curves of DHFR samples. Table 1 lists kinetic parameters and dissociation constants. Figure S1 shows GLN matrices of split DHFR and cat-DHFR. Figure S3 shows constructs with split-intein pairs on the same side. Figure S4 shows the effect of linker length on yield.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of DHFR. 2. The strongest evidence is the retention of catalytic activity and enhanced stability. 3. The future path is using directed evolution to restore or surpass linear control activity.
